findings.title: Rendering an HTML altChunk can exhaust host memory through colspan
findings.summary: Rendering a DOCX whose HTML altChunk contains a very large `colspan` builds one XML grid column per requested span. A tiny input can request billions of columns and exhaust the rendering process before layout; archive and XML input budgets do not bound this generated output.

severity.rationale: An untrusted document author can force process-wide CPU and memory exhaustion through ordinary PDF/PNG/report rendering, including an embedding Python host. Delivery requires a caller to render the document; no remote service deployment or broader compromise is established. Process memory/CPU limits recommended by SECURITY.md reduce the blast radius.
severity.changeConditions: A shared rendering service accepting arbitrary uploads would raise likelihood; an enforced worker memory/time/output bound would reduce impact.

confidence.rationale: Direct source trace proves unbounded decimal span parsing and the exact proportional output loop after admission. No exploit or runtime workload was executed.

taxonomy.category: Uncontrolled resource consumption during HTML-to-OOXML expansion

codeEvidence.label: Rendering expands the embedded chunk after admission
codeEvidence.explanation: The document author selects an internal HTML relationship; its bytes are expanded before DOM/layout and without an output budget.

codeEvidence.label: Chunk bytes flow into the HTML builder
codeEvidence.explanation: The referenced embedded part is decoded as HTML/MHT and converted by html_to_wml; no semantic table-span limit is applied.

codeEvidence.label: Untrusted colspan has no upper bound
codeEvidence.explanation: Any positive usize from an HTML cell is retained as span; only invalid and zero values are normalized.

codeEvidence.label: Spans determine the generated column count
codeEvidence.code:
let cols = table
            .rows
            .iter()
            .map(|r| r.iter().map(|c| c.span).sum::<usize>())
            .max()
            .unwrap_or(1)
            .max(1);
        let col_w = 9360 / cols;
codeEvidence.explanation: The largest row sum directly becomes cols, independently of source byte length; one cell can set it to one billion.

codeEvidence.label: One XML allocation append per attacker-requested column
codeEvidence.explanation: The unbounded loop appends a full gridCol string for every requested column. A billion-column span attempts tens of gigabytes of XML before any later layout guard.

rootCause.summary: The HTML cell parser accepts an arbitrary positive `usize` as `colspan`. `end_table` sums those values into `cols` and writes one `w:gridCol` per column into an in-memory String. The initial package admission occurs before this HTML transformation and controls original ZIP/XML bytes, while generated XML and semantic table dimensions are unbounded.

findings.remediation: Reject excessive per-cell spans and cumulative table-column counts with checked arithmetic before expansion, and enforce a generated-XML byte budget during altChunk conversion. Return a structured conversion refusal instead of attempting the output.

counterEvidence: Archive admission bounds compressed/inflated original bytes; this does not limit post-admission expansion.
SECURITY.md recommends separate process CPU/memory limits; this can contain a worker but does not reject the input in the library.
External relationships are not required; the payload resides in the DOCX.
limitations: Static validation only; no malicious document was generated or rendered.
Deployment exposure and host resource limits are unknown.
validation.summary: Parent checked the chunk loader, HTML token dispatch, span parsing and table closure. A small internal HTML table with `colspan="1000000000"` reaches the proportional append loop after package admission. Existing tests normalize zero/invalid spans but impose no positive upper bound.

dataflow.summary: Caller-controlled DOCX -> with_layout -> internal altChunk bytes -> html_to_wml -> Builder::start colspan -> end_table cols -> String grid-column append loop.

impact.why: Potential process termination through unbounded allocation, including the host embedding the library.

likelihood.why: Source supports ordinary rendering reachability; deployment frequency and process isolation are unknown.

reachability.summary: An attacker controls a document submitted to a caller of the public conversion APIs. Rendering requires no special flag for altChunk expansion. The resulting exhaustion affects the renderer process; no remote endpoint is assumed.
reachability.entrypoint: DOCX rendering APIs (PDF, PNG and render reports)
reachability.outcome: CPU and memory exhaustion before document layout.
preconditions: A consumer renders the attacker-supplied DOCX.

attackPath.summary: Supply a small DOCX with an internal HTML altChunk containing a table cell with a very large positive colspan, then have a caller request PDF, PNG or a render report.

remediationTests: Reject a very large positive colspan before emitting grid columns.
Reject cumulative row-span overflow and excessive summed columns.
Verify normal small spans and zero/invalid-span fallback remain correct.
Verify rendering a DOCX carrying the oversized altChunk returns a bounded error.

originalEvidence.description: Baseline reports unbounded usize colspan from HTML altChunk is summed into table columns and emitted one gridCol per span. Small embedded HTML can request a billion columns; parent validation pending.

findings.title: Renaming a related XML part can crash DOCX rendering
findings.summary: A document can place deeply nested font-table XML in `word/fontTable.bin` and select it with an internal fontTable relationship. Admission applies XML depth and attribute policy only to `.xml`/`.rels` filenames (with an exception for the main part), while the font-table consumer parses the renamed part recursively without checking the policy. Rendering can therefore exhaust the process stack despite passing admission.

severity.rationale: An untrusted document author can terminate a rendering process, including its native library host, by controlling an internal auxiliary part and its relationship. The input can be small and needs no raised limits. A consumer must render the document; remote exposure is not established and process isolation limits collateral effects.
severity.changeConditions: Shared multi-user rendering without process isolation would raise likelihood; checked parsing at each consumer would eliminate the bypass.

confidence.rationale: Independent static review confirms the filename-based admission branch, explicit nonstandard auxiliary part resolution and unchecked recursive parse. Crash depth is platform/stack dependent; no exploit was run.

taxonomy.category: XML policy bypass through inconsistent part classification

codeEvidence.label: Filename selects whether XML policy runs
codeEvidence.explanation: A `.bin` auxiliary XML entry is inflated and byte-counted but never passed to check_xml_depth, which also enforces tag policy.

codeEvidence.label: Only the main part gets a semantic fallback scan
codeEvidence.explanation: Admission explicitly repairs the extension mismatch for the main document, but does not inspect semantic auxiliary XML targets.

codeEvidence.label: Relationship target selects a freely named auxiliary part
codeEvidence.explanation: An internal fontTable relationship can select `fontTable.bin`; there is no filename suffix restriction at the consuming boundary.

codeEvidence.label: Font-table consumer uses the unchecked DOM parser
codeEvidence.explanation: The related part is converted to text and parsed without try_parse_xdocument or an active InputLimits check.

codeEvidence.label: Nested input recursively consumes the native stack
codeEvidence.explanation: Unchecked parsing recurses once per nested element with no depth bound, so an auxiliary part bypassing admission can exhaust the host stack.

codeEvidence.label: Ordinary rendering loads the font table
codeEvidence.code:
let table = font_table::load_font_table(&pkg);
    let mut embedded = font_table::load_embedded_fonts(&pkg, &table);
codeEvidence.explanation: The shared layout pipeline always reaches this consumer after package admission and normalization, without a feature flag.

rootCause.summary: Admission identifies XML by filename, whereas rendering identifies the font table by an internal relationship type. The latter permits arbitrary part names. A non-XML-suffixed font-table target therefore receives only byte limits, then `load_font_table` sends it into the deliberately unchecked recursive DOM parser. The main-part fallback scan does not cover this auxiliary consumer.

findings.remediation: Enforce active XML limits at every XML consumer regardless of part extension, or have admission discover all semantically XML related/content-typed parts. Pass limits through the font-table loader and use checked parsing before DOM construction.

counterEvidence: Normal `.xml` font tables are policy-checked at admission.
The unchecked DOM API is intentionally documented for trusted/prevalidated input; the flaw is the package-level bypass reaching it.
Original package byte/entry and local-header controls still apply and do not prevent a small, deeply nested auxiliary XML payload.
limitations: No runtime crash was induced; exact exhaustion depth depends on target stack size.
Sibling auxiliary consumers are being reconciled; this finding establishes the font-table path.
validation.summary: Parent verified the admission branch and main-only exception, related-part resolver and font-table load, strict-normalization filename check, bounded PartFs byte loader and unchecked parser recursion. None supplies a depth check for a `.bin` font-table target.

dataflow.summary: DOCX ZIP/relationships -> suffix-based admission skips auxiliary XML policy -> main_rel_part(fontTable) resolves `.bin` -> load_font_table -> parse_xdocument -> recursive parse_element.

impact.why: Native process stack exhaustion can terminate the embedding host.

likelihood.why: Ordinary conversion is reachable from document input, but actual deployment isolation is unknown.

reachability.summary: A document author controls the related part name, relationship and contents. A caller rendering the package crosses into the native recursive parser; no privileged caller setting or remote-service assumption is needed.
reachability.outcome: Renderer or embedding process termination through stack exhaustion.

attackPath.summary: Provide a DOCX whose internal fontTable relationship points to a non-XML-suffixed part containing deeply nested XML, then request rendering.

remediationTests: Reject an over-depth font table targeted under a `.bin` name through an internal relationship.
Apply attribute/tag limits to renamed auxiliary XML parts.
Keep valid nonstandard auxiliary names supported while enforcing the same XML policy.
Exercise equivalent settings, styles, numbering and story consumers for filename-independent policy enforcement.

candidate.title: WMF polygon record ignores record end for attacker count

originalEvidence.description: Investigator lead: global WMF record-size validation is not used to bound polygon/text reads; short records each claim 65,535 points and reread following file bytes, amplifying CPU. Exact source trace pending.
originalEvidence.additional: META_EXTTEXTOUT src/convert/metafile.rs:604-612 takes n=65535 from whole data rather than record-local end; repeated short records each retain overlapping 65535-byte strings in texts. META_POLYGON similarly amplifies CPU.
